newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Political feud cripples Nigerian oil town.
newsitem.headline: Political feud cripples Nigerian oil town.

text.p: Business is at a standstill in Warri, a Nigerian oil town popularly called "Jungle City" where political feuding led to seizure of Shell oil stations and bloody riots this month.

Residents said the trouble was set off by charges of fraud in municipal council polls two weeks ago against a backdrop of tribal rivalries. Rampaging youths took over the streets and a teenage girl died in the violence.

Then Ijaw tribesmen, angry with the military government for relocating their local council headquarters to a rival town, invaded the Shell stations last weekend and took 127 Nigerian oil workers of the company hostage.
All have now been freed, the last batch of 52 on Thursday.

"Many of our markets have been operating intermittently for the past weeks while some were shut down since Tuesday to avoid further looting, burning and destruction of goods by troublesome youths," Julie Osiobe, a textiles trader at the Warri central market, told Reuters on Thursday.
Cynthia Ese, one of dozens of women held by the police for soliciting, said there was no more business because the city was "dead and quiet".
"Since the crisis escalated, I haven't operated beyond six p.m. and I'm the only one working," said Pessu Ajaero, owner of Chic's, a popular drinking spot in Warri.
His workers from the warring tribes had gone into hiding for fear of reprisals, he said.

Warri, dubbed "Jungle City" because of its chaotic traffic, rampant crime and crowded roads, is located in the midwest and is the western operational headquarters for Shell, the biggest oil producer in Nigeria.
At the root of the crisis in Warri area is a rivalry among three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and the Urhobos.
The Urhobos controlled affairs there in the 1970s until the Itsekiris, who provide the paramount ruler for Warri, began to press for more say in the town in the 1980s.
The Ijaws, who inhabit the riverine areas and have a bigger population also began asking for more amenities in their areas.

Residents said there was rioting most of this week by Ijaw and Itsekiri youths who attacked homes of ethnic leaders and popular spots in retaliatory measures. Sporadic shooting was also heard and three Ijaw tribesmen died in the riots.

Two weeks ago, a handful of Urhobo youths had taken to the streets to protest against the defeat of their aspiring chairman during the municipal polls. They alleged that rigging had given victory to a rival candidate of the Itsekiri tribe.
The municipal council polls were part of the Nigerian military government's transition plan it says will restore democracy next year.
"Two weeks ago, we closed our businesses because the youths used the period as an opportunity to plunder and loot," said Okoro Oshare, who owns a vehicle spare parts shop.
James Diata, Warri divisional police officer, said the city had not recovered from the council poll crisis when Ijaws and Itsekiris began their own troubles.
"But we tried to handle both cases well...Some policemen are also manning the markets and other trouble spots. We also have over 100 anti-riots troops on stand-by at the city outskirts," Diata said.

The communities in Warri, like those in other oil-producing areas, have long been restive over the perception that the oil wealth derived from their land is used in other parts of the vast nation or ends up in the pockets of the elite.
